_about: Completed-print lines that need no facts at all: the last resort that always fits.

entries.text: The printer has an extruder because apparently the household needed another mouth to feed.
The Industrial Revolution was a little more convincing when it made locomotives.
Wall Street calls it a depreciating asset; the filament aisle calls it a recurring customer.
The printer is the only employee in the house that gets paid in plastic and never requests a raise.
Your hobby has achieved vertical integration by producing both the clutter and the containers for it.
The slicer calculated the material requirement but wisely omitted the emotional cost of explaining the purchase.
The printer has turned retail therapy into a home manufacturing initiative.
A silicon chip just spent hours turning chemistry into something the dollar store would put near the register.
You have acquired the ability to manufacture nearly anything and the restraint of an unattended shopping cart.
The printer is like a vending machine that charges for the snack, the machine and the engineering consultation.
The first law of thermodynamics has nothing to say about the conservation of disposable income.
The printer is doing what economists call stimulating demand, mostly for additional printer parts.
A home factory is impressive until you realize the factory has a better social calendar than its products.
The next firmware update should include an accountant who refuses to enable the extruder until the budget balances.
The nozzle moves at hundreds of millimeters per second while the household's financial goals remain stationary.
The printer has finally democratized the manufacturing of things nobody was previously willing to manufacture.
Even IKEA makes you leave the house before it starts assigning homework.
The machine has brought manufacturing jobs back to America without creating a single paying position.
Somewhere a spreadsheet just saw the equipment depreciation schedule and closed itself.
The best feature of additive manufacturing is that the subtraction happens automatically in your bank account.
Calibration is the process of ensuring the machine can waste money with repeatable precision.
A 3D printer is an appliance that makes its own accessories and still somehow requires a shopping account.
The slicer estimates print time with the optimism of a contractor renovating your bathroom.
Infill is a wonderful way to make the inside of your financial mistake look sophisticated.
The printer has solved the problem of idle hands by giving them something expensive to supervise.
Support material is the only employee that gets fired specifically for doing its job.
The first layer is a job interview conducted entirely on the floor.
A spool is a subscription service whose cancellation policy involves running out of plastic.
A brim is the printer's security deposit, refundable in tiny sharp pieces.
The nozzle is a very small hole through which a surprisingly large retirement account can pass.
The build plate has more scheduled maintenance than the person responsible for scheduling it.
Firmware updates are the printer's way of announcing that yesterday's problems were merely introductory.
Your printer's camera has turned a manufacturing process into the world's slowest reality show.
A filament dryer is a luxury sauna for the one household possession that cannot appreciate it.
The printer has given ordinary citizens the opportunity to experience supply chain problems in their own homes.
A slicer is a computer program that translates enthusiasm into utility bills.
The extruder is the world's smallest cash register with the world's longest checkout process.
A productive weekend for the printer involves sitting around and assembling an expensive sandwich of layers.
A multicolor print is a beautiful argument against the idea that garbage should be monochromatic.
The printer is the only household appliance that can turn a software update into a mechanical engineering degree.
A printer launders money into frogs with surprisingly little interest from the Treasury Department.
Three hobbies: printing, repairing the printer, and explaining why buying it wasn't a mistake.
A two dollar hook lacks the intellectual challenge of spending six dollars making one.
The printer has a silent mode, which is unfortunately not available for the person explaining the latest upgrade.
Engineers call it tolerance because acceptance would imply everybody was happy with the result.
The difference between a print farm and a regular farm is that the chickens don't require monthly firmware updates.
The nozzle has a smaller opening than the gap between the projected and actual budget.
My favorite part of open source hardware is how quickly it opens the wallet.
A filament runout sensor is a tiny mechanical device for detecting when the shopping cart needs attention.
The printer's resume lists precision manufacturing, continuous improvement, and an inexplicable gap in financial responsibility.
A print farm's most successful crop is the cardboard box each new spool arrives in.
The heated bed is the only bed in the house that gets perfectly leveled before anyone can use it.
The purge line is the machine's little reminder that even the introduction to this project costs money.
Nobody tells you that a multicolor printer is basically an oil painting that invoices you for the paintbrush.
A good spool goes to the extruder; a bad spool goes on an internet forum for three weeks of discussion.
The reason filament comes in kilograms is that financial regret is easier to process in metric.
A printer enclosure is a padded room for the only participant in this hobby that isn't losing its mind.
A bed mesh is a topographic map of the tiny patch of Earth your printer considers uninhabitable.
The machine has a factory reset, but the credit card company refuses to implement a matching feature.
A factory making replacement parts for itself is one awkward meeting away from becoming a government department.
Your slicer has fifty ways to calculate a wall and your house still needs painting.
The printer's version of self care is unloading a perfectly good roll and demanding a different color.
A support blocker is a tool that finally lets you tell something to stop helping.
The printer has a fan club, although most of its members are bolted to the frame.
The Z axis is the only thing in this hobby that knows when to stop going up.
A spool holder is the printer's snack tray and a remarkable opportunity to spend more on the snack tray.
The printer's hot end is called that because calling it a financial exhaust pipe would interfere with sales.
Every printer comes with a warranty, a user manual, and an unspoken invitation to invalidate both.
You can measure print quality with calipers, but the justification requires a creative writing degree.
The hobby has taught me that a hole in a model can cost more than the material surrounding it.
The filament aisle has better customer retention than an airline and considerably more legroom.
A calibration print is the manufacturing equivalent of buying a second bathroom scale to investigate the first.
If the machine could print a new debit card, the financial ecosystem would finally be complete.
The extruder has one job and a larger collection of spare parts than the engine of my car.
The only thing more addictive than downloading free models is buying hardware to make them slightly faster.
The printer's startup sequence has more self confidence than its owner's investment portfolio.
A slicer knows the exact volume of a plastic object but has no vocabulary for the word enough.
The 3D printing industry calls the machine a tool because calling it an expensive personality trait would hurt sales.
Every successful print is accompanied by the discovery of a previously unimaginable need for another print.
The American dream used to involve home ownership; now it apparently involves owning a machine that makes tiny houses.
A printer with artificial intelligence will eventually tell you to buy a commercially available version and be done with it.
The printer has a screen, camera, and WiFi so naturally you watch it from another screen.
The hot end can reach hundreds of degrees, but it can't warm the reception your receipts get at home.
A hobby that requires a humidity sensor has accidentally become a weather station with a shopping problem.
A 3D printer is the perfect appliance for anyone who believes a receipt should come with a sequel.
Some people collect stamps because they understand the important principle of objects that occupy very little space.
A heated chamber is what happens when an expensive machine acquires a climate controlled penthouse.
The printer detects spaghetti earlier than its owner detects a bad purchase.
A layer height of one tenth of a millimeter means regret can now be delivered with remarkable precision.
The camera can watch the printer from anywhere in the world, providing absolutely no reason to go anywhere.
The slicer is a travel agent whose most popular destination is the hardware store.
Every millimeter of extra clearance is an admission that the laws of geometry have excellent legal representation.
A resin printer is a machine that requires protective gloves to handle the consequences of your purchasing decisions.
The nozzle is a tiny industrial fountain dispensing the liquid form of your discretionary income.
A printer's auto leveling feature is a remarkably complicated way to confirm that the table you bought is crooked.
The filament is wound into a circle because the manufacturer knows perfectly well where you'll be going next.
The printer's advantage over a factory is that its unpaid labor volunteers for overtime.
The machine has an emergency stop, which is more restraint than the online filament store is legally required to offer.
A print queue is a to do list for a machine that has already eaten your free time.
You bought a printer to solve problems, so the printer very thoughtfully started supplying them.
The only component that consistently stays within its specified tolerance is the price of the replacement component.
The printer measures temperature to a decimal place but nobody calibrated the buyer's remorse sensor.
A spool of translucent filament is a transparent attempt to hide a transaction from the household budget.
Even the printer's standby mode has a better work life balance than somebody watching a first layer.
The easiest way to identify a printing enthusiast is to ask where their dining table went.
Power loss recovery is a feature conspicuously absent from your retirement account.
The filament store has developed an impressive business by selling circular objects to people going in circles.
A print bed is the world's smallest construction site with the world's most dedicated unpaid site inspector.
The printer has never asked for an employee discount, which proves machines still have a lot to learn.
The best thing about mechanical upgrades is how often they introduce entirely new noises to diagnose.
The first layer is the machine's opening statement, and the rest of the print is remarkably expensive testimony.
The slicer has a setting for ironing, because even molten plastic is apparently expected to look presentable for company.
A printed replacement part is the industrial version of borrowing money to pay off your own loan.
The machine is capable of producing a miniature Eiffel Tower while the actual laundry still needs folding.
The printer's pause button is a temporary truce between the electricity company and the filament supplier.
An empty spool is the world's most accurate pie chart of a completely exhausted resource.
The nozzle cleans itself before each job, which makes it the most hygienic employee in the workshop.
A printer with four filament slots is simply a cash register that offers four simultaneous payment options.
I would calculate the return on investment, but the calculator probably needs a custom printed case first.
The printer's greatest achievement is making a person excited about a notification from an appliance.
That support material used more filament than the actual intended part.
You bought a high-speed printer just to accumulate plastic trinkets even faster.
The nozzle dragged through that top layer like a rake across gravel.
Every completed print brings us closer to being buried under melted polymer.
That model has the geometry of an apology delivered way too late.
The cooling duct blew bravely against the tide of sheer aesthetic failure.
Somewhere, a store shelf feels quietly threatened by this operation.
The printer did the work and the human took the bow, as tradition demands.
Another object exists because a rectangle of plastic believed in itself.
This hobby started as one print and nobody can locate the exit anymore.
Layers were stacked, time was spent, and dignity remains mostly intact.
A finished print is just a download that committed to real estate.
The build plate giveth, and the build plate occasionally stringeth.
Every great shelf begins with a single questionable download.
Plastic was warmed, moved precisely, and promoted to object status.
The most reliable narrator in this house is a finished print.
Nobody is saying it is a problem; the shelf is saying it, silently.
From spool to showpiece, with only minor supervising from the couch.
A printer's favorite sentence is the one that ends with cooldown.
The object is done and the next object is already being considered.
Proof that patience, heat, and software can agree on something.
